newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-STANKOWSKI LEADS BAY HILL, WOODS AND JONES ONE SHOT BACK.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-STANKOWSKI LEADS BAY HILL, WOODS AND JONES ONE SHOT BACK.

text.p: Paul Stankowski shot a five-under-par 67 Thursday to take a one-stroke lead over Tiger Woods, U.S. Open champion Steve Jones and two other golfers after the first round of the Bay Hill Invitational.
Also in second place at four under were Billy Andrade and Fred Funk. Nine players were at three under including former Bay Hill winners Payne Stewart, Tom Kite and defending champion Paul Goydos.

Stankowski, already a winner this year at the Hawaiian Open and the second-round leader last week at the Honda Classic, said his opening round at Bay Hill was his best ball-striking round of the year.

"I'm especially pleased with how I placed my iron shots. I've been struggling with iron placement, and having a lot of 25 footers, but today I was hitting it close," said Stankowski, whose only bogey came from a rare missed green on Thursday.

As if further evidence were needed of the difference between Tiger Woods and other golfers, the 21-year-old, after finishing the round just a stroke off the lead without a bogey, said it was one of his worst ball-striking rounds of the year.

"I didn't hit it well at all, missed a lot of fairways, and wasn't sharp with my irons," said Woods. "But I grinded it around and got it in the hole somehow. Those are great rounds, when you don't play well but can get into the clubhouse with a good score and not shoot yourself out of the tournament."
Woods spent the last two weeks off, relaxing and practicing. "I was itching to play when I started today," he said. "I was more than ready.
"Even though I'm not pleased with the way I did play, the great thing is that I know what I'm doing wrong, it'll be just a matter of getting it out of my system tomorrow on the range."

Though there was no wind on Thursday and the course was in perfect condition, scores were generally high. "This is the easiest you'll ever see it. It just shows you what a good test it is," said Jones.

Course designer Arnold Palmer, playing in his first tournament since surgery for prostate cancer, shot a round of nine-over 81. His biggest trouble came just before the turn, when he double bogeyed the eighth hole an tripled the ninth.

"Actually, it was as solid as I've hit the ball in a couple of years. I felt very lucky just to be out there playing. I feel good though, so good I could play another 18 right now," said Palmer soon after his round.
